Era I, each one its own

All twenty era-I buildings, each under its own roofing material and carrying one object that breaks its own roofline and belongs to no other building.

First, at the size the map actually draws them

A render viewed at 700 px always looks fine. These are the same files laid on the real ground at the two zooms a player gets, which is where a design either reads or does not.

0.80 — the closest the map will go. A 3 × 3 building is 154 px wide here.

0.35 — a working distance. Everything still has to be recognisable from its silhouette alone.

The roster

Each preset is named for its building_defs id, so --preset storehouse renders exactly what storehouse will show on the map.

Castle

A castle is a HOUSEHOLD before it is a fortification: the kitchen fire is lit, the washing is out, birds sit on the wall-head and there is a bench by the gate for whoever is waiting.

main_hall 5 × 5 the seat

Breeding Hut

The jettied upper floor and the withy pen: a nest, an egg, something small already out of it, and the parents underfoot.

breeding_hut 4 × 4 creatures

Small House

A cottage: cruck frame, wattle panels, deep thatch pegged down along the ridge, a smoking chimney and a fenced garden — and the creatures live in the garden, where a cottager’s animals did.

hut 3 × 3 dwelling

Large House

A LONGHOUSE, which is the one medieval building that is long by definition: one ridge the whole way, a cross-passage with a door each side, people at one end and the byre at the other.

house 2 × 5 dwelling

Small Wood Camp

A SPAR TREE: topped, barked, its limbs cut to stubs and the climbing rope still coiled round it. A woodpile says timber; a topped spar says felling, and it stands taller than anything else in the camp.

wood_camp_e1 4 × 3 gathering

Small Stone Camp

The derrick, LOADED — a dressed block hanging in its sling over the quarry face, with the windlass at its foot. An empty boom is three poles that fell together.

stone_camp_e1 4 × 3 gathering

Large Wood Camp

A WATER WHEEL, and it is the whole argument for this pass: nothing else in the settlement is a circle standing on edge, so it is read before the hall it is bolted to, at any zoom, with no prop visible.

wood_works_e1 4 × 4 refining

Large Stone Camp

The same quarry at twice the size, worked by two gangs: a second face cut into the left wall with its own mouth, its own crane and its own track.

stone_works_e1 4 × 4 refining

Storehouse

A GABLE HOIST at the ridge with a sack halfway up the rope, over thatch and staddle stones. Every granary had one and nothing else did.

storehouse 4 × 3 storage

Gold Vault

A CHAIN right round the tower and a padlock the size of the door, under a black iron spire. Bars say defended; a chain says shut.

gold_vault 3 × 3 storage

Builder Camp

A TREADWHEEL CRANE over the scaffold and an arch half-turned on its timber centring — together they say the one thing the yard is for: something is going up, and it is not finished.

builder_camp 3 × 4 civic

Healing Hut

A STILL — copper pot, swan neck, condenser in a water tub, steam coming off it — under a turf roof with flowers growing in it. A cauldron on a fire is a kitchen; this is a laboratory.

healing_hut 3 × 3 civic

Scout Post

A BEACON in an iron cage above the spire, lit and smoking. A brazier on the deck warms your hands; the same fire lifted over everything is a signal.

scout_post 2 × 2 civic

Trade Center

A GREAT BALANCE beside the stalls: every other market prop is a thing being sold, and this is the thing that settles the price.

trading_post 4 × 3 civic

Caravanserai

A striped PAVILION in the yard — the tent the caravan brought with it, and the only cloth roof on the map. Around it the beasts, the wagons and the fodder.

caravanserai 4 × 3 civic

Hatchery

A shell-white DOME with a louvre on top for the heat to leave by — the one roof shape nothing else on the map has, and it is also the egg. A giant one sits in its cradle below.

hatchery 4 × 3 creatures

Fish Hut

A NET slung between two masts with the floats and the catch in it, over a slate roof and a dock cut into the plinth with the boat floating in it.

lux_fish 3 × 3 luxury

Fur Lodge

A BEAR on a hoop as wide as the lodge is tall — the darkest thing on the map inside a pale withy frame — and an antler rack on its own post. Roofed in hides.

lux_fur 3 × 3 luxury

Marketplace

A PLACE, not a building. Paving, a market cross, four cloth stalls, a well and a money-changer’s table — the only roofs on it are canvas.

special_treasury_e1 4 × 4 monument

Church

A nave five cells long with a west tower — proportion is what makes a church read as a church from above. Copper roof, belfry stage you can see through, spire, churchyard.

special_materials_e1 3 × 5 monument

What changed, and why

Seven passes: Roman to medieval fantasy, props that name each building, footprints chosen for the design, inhabitants, finer blocks, roofs and colour — and now a signature apiece.

The dimension nothing was using

Every prop that NAMES a building lived in its yard: at ground level, at prop scale, behind a fence. Zoom out and that whole layer becomes texture and the roof becomes the picture — which is how twenty buildings could still resolve to one building with twenty roofs. Height was free the whole time. It costs no ground, nothing is ever standing in it, and a shape above the ridge is the LAST thing to disappear as the camera pulls back.

One per building, and no more

Two signatures is a style; one is a name. So each building gets exactly one object that breaks its own roofline and could be bolted onto no other building on the map — a wheel, a chain, a beacon, a bear, a balance, an egg. Everything else in the yard stays where it was and goes back to being what it always was: the evidence that somebody works here.

The two that had to be separated

The masons had a treadwheel crane and the carpenters next door have a mill wheel, and A BIG WHEEL on both put the pair that was already the hardest to tell apart straight back into one silhouette. The crane was not wrong, it was in the wrong yard: it moved to the Builder Camp, where a jib over a half-built wall is what the place is FOR, and the lodge got the one thing only a lodge makes.

A quarter turn, five times over

Every circle here is n boxes placed round a hub, and the first pass turned each box by the bearing of its own position — which points its long axis at the centre. The wheel came out a sunburst, the hoop a spiky flower, the coin a cog. The tangent is a quarter turn off the radius and a box has no idea which way round it is, so the offset has to be added by hand; it is written down once now, derived rather than guessed, in two functions with the derivation in the comment.

Being on your own roof is not being off your own tile

The antler rack was nailed over the door. Between the door head at 0.98 and the eave at 1.22 there is a quarter of a metre and a rack is half of one, so every tine ended up lying on the roof slope behind it. The footprint check cannot see that — it measures ground, and the rack was over its own ground the whole time. Only the render found it, which is why the render is part of the loop and not the end of it.

Five last roofs

Copper gone green for the minster, gilt for the treasury, black iron for the vault, shell-white for the hatchery, southern pantile for the caravanserai. With those, no two buildings in the settlement are roofed the same way — which was the point of the roof pass and is only now actually true.

The footprints are the roster’s, not free choices. The art contract is that a building’s base is exactly gridW × gridH cells wide, so a model built to a different plan arrives on the map standing on ground it does not own and refusing taps on ground it does. The freedom went into the plans instead — where the yard sits, which way a gable turns, what is left open to the sky.

Renders live in docs/renders/. Building art is served from image_url, so these still need uploading through Dev Mode — unlike the roads, which ship bundled because a road needs sixteen pictures rather than one.
